A quidnunc is a person who is obsessively, restlessly curious about the latest news, gossip, and other people's business — and who can't help but talk about it constantly.

Think of that one person you know who always seems to know everything that's happening with everyone, always has the "latest scoop," and is perpetually fishing for new information to share or spread. That person is a quidnunc.

A quidnunc has two inseparable qualities working together:

1. An insatiable hunger for information about others. A quidnunc is not merely curious — they are compulsively curious. They need to know what's going on in the neighborhood, in the office, in other people's relationships, in the news. The not-knowing genuinely bothers them. They ask probing questions, eavesdrop, lurk around conversations, and keep their ears permanently open.

2. A compulsion to spread what they learn. A quidnunc rarely keeps information to themselves. The whole point, for them, is to be the person "in the know" — and ideally, to be the one who tells others. They derive satisfaction from being the source. They pass along rumors, updates, and stories, often without checking whether any of it is true or whether it's even their business to share.

Together, these two qualities make a quidnunc essentially a gossip machine — constantly collecting and redistributing information about the world around them, especially information about other people.

Quidnunc is not a compliment. It carries a distinctly negative, mocking tone. When you call someone a quidnunc, you are gently (or not so gently) criticizing them for being a nosy, meddlesome gossip. The word suggests that the person has made prying into others' affairs into something of a hobby or even a lifestyle.

That said, it's not a vicious insult. It's more of a wry, somewhat old-fashioned, literary dig — the kind of word a witty person might use to describe an insufferable town gossip with a raised eyebrow and a hint of amusement.
How It Differs from Just Being Curious

Ordinary curiosity is healthy and admirable. A quidnunc's curiosity is neither of those things. Here's the difference:

A curious person wants to understand the world — ideas, science, art, how things work. A quidnunc's curiosity is narrow and personal: they want to know what's happening with specific people, and specifically the kind of information those people may not want widely known. Their curiosity is also unrelenting — it doesn't get satisfied, it just moves on to the next piece of gossip. And crucially, their goal isn't understanding; it's social currency — the thrill of knowing and telling.

• The neighbor who always seems to know when someone on the street got divorced, who's having money trouble, and who just came back from a holiday — and makes sure everyone else knows too. Quidnunc.
  • The coworker who hovers near conversations they weren't invited to, asks unnecessary follow-up questions about your personal life, and is somehow always the first to know about any office drama. Quidnunc.
  • The relative at family gatherings who interrogates everyone about their relationships, careers, and finances — and then reports those answers to others across the room. Quidnunc.

• "Don't tell Margaret anything you want kept private — she's the biggest quidnunc in the village."
  • "He positioned himself near the reception desk, playing the quidnunc as usual, collecting every scrap of gossip he could."
  • "The town quidnunc had already spread three different versions of the story before the truth was even established."
A quidnunc is a nosy, gossipy person who is always desperate to know — and talk about — the latest news and other people's business. The word mocks them gently but clearly.
